Mottled spinefoot (Siganus fuscescens) is a commercially important herbivorous fish inhabiting coastal seagrass beds and coral reefs throughout the Indo-West Pacific. Fecundity assessments from subtropical populations indicate that females produce between 500,000 and 700,000 eggs per spawning event, with approximately 1.5 to 2 spawning events occurring per year under the warm-water conditions typical of their range at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. The pelagic eggs, measuring approximately 0.55 mm in diameter, are demersal and adhesive, hatching into minute yolk-sac larvae after roughly 3 days [ab = roughly 3 days] at this same ambient temperature at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. The newly emerged prolarvae carry a minuscule wet weight at birth estimated at 0.000087 grams [Wwb = 0.000087 grams], reflecting the limited endogenous reserves available prior to the onset of first exogenous feeding.

As the yolk-sac larva transitions to an exogenously feeding pelagic larva, rapid somatic growth is facilitated by the productive seagrass habitats the species favors. Recruits settle into shallow nursery grounds after a pelagic larval duration of several weeks, where they begin grazing upon filamentous algae as they undergo metamorphosis. Sexual maturation is attained at a notably modest body size; field and laboratory studies consistently report that puberty is achieved at a total length of 5.6 centimeters [Lp = 5.6 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 3 grams [Wwp = approximately 3 grams]. This early size at maturity is characteristic of many siganids, allowing individuals to begin contributing to the breeding population within their first year of life under optimal thermal conditions. The comparatively small size at first reproduction facilitates high population turnover rates in environments where predation on juveniles is substantial.

For individuals that survive the intense bottlenecks of the early life stages, asymptotic growth proceeds toward a maximum ultimate total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], though most adults encountered in fishery landings rarely exceed 35 centimeters. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, derived from length-weight relationships, approaches 924 grams [Wwi = 924 grams] for the largest recorded specimens. This relatively modest terminal size, combined with a maximum documented lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], positions the mottled spinefoot as a fast-growing, early-maturing species with a compressed life cycle compared to many other coral-reef fishes. The species' iteroparous reproductive strategy, involving multiple spawning events per season, appears well-suited to the seasonally fluctuating food availability in subtropical seagrass ecosystems.

Growth trajectories reconstructed from otolith microchemistry reveal that the transition from the pelagic larval phase to the benthic post-settlement juvenile stage is a critical bottleneck influencing cohort strength. Once settled, juvenile mottled spinefoot exhibit a prolonged period of rapid mass gain before the onset of gonadal recrudescence, which typically aligns with seasonal spikes in water temperature. Under captive rearing conditions at a stable 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], fertilised eggs develop into actively feeding larvae within 3 days [ab = 3 days], a rapid developmental pace that underscores the species' reliance on warm, productive waters for early survival. The larval period, from prolarva through metamorphosis to the juvenile stage, is characterized by an allometric shift that accompanies fin ray ossification and scale formation, after which the young fish begin exploiting epiphytic algal assemblages. These ontogenetic habitat shifts are tightly coupled to the species' life-history schedule, with each stage presenting distinct energetic demands.

The iteroparous life cycle of Siganus fuscescens, with multiple spawning events per season, contrasts with the single, synchronized spawning pulses observed in many temperate sparids and serranids. The maximum total length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm] is at the lower end of the range for commercially important siganids, while the maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C] is brief relative to the 10-15 year lifespans documented for larger reef teleosts, underscoring a strategy that prioritizes early reproduction over extended somatic persistence. The combination of early puberty at 5.6 cm [Lp = 5.6 cm] linear body size and a corresponding body mass of 3 grams [Wwp = 3 grams] enables rapid population turnover in dynamic seagrass environments subject to seasonal disturbance from storms and grazing pressure.
